threads.topic: What happened to the LOBOs on 22 July 2026

entries.q: The 2025-26 outturn report went to Council on 22 July 2026 saying the LOBO call right 'may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026' — which was 22 July, the same day. Was the option exercised on the £19.25m, and if the loans were repaid, at what rate were they replaced?
entries.why: The LOBOs cost 4.65%. PWLB 10-year is currently around 6%. On £19.25m that is roughly £264,000 a year, and it will have been decided before this committee next sits. The outturn does not carry the outcome because the paper was tabled on the day.

entries.q: Wolverhampton reports three LOBO calls in 2025-26 where lenders proposed 6.19%, 6.21% and 6.26% against existing rates of 3.60%, 4.26% and 4.29%. It rejected all three and repaid £17.0m, having built the possibility into its cashflow in advance.
entries.why: That is the shape of the decision Bridgend faced on 22 July on £19.25m at 4.65%. A lender calling is generally offering a rate set to be refused, so the practical question is whether the cash was ready to repay — not whether the new rate was acceptable.

threads.topic: Two thirds of the cash is lent to other councils

entries.q: £30.00m of £44.50m of investments — 67% — sits with other local authorities, none of which carry a credit rating. What is the largest single exposure, and what would trigger a reduction in the local authority allocation?
entries.why: The strategy relies on councils being secure counterparties. That is generally right and has never been tested at a section 114 authority, which is precisely why the concentration limit matters more than the average rate.

entries.q: 2026-27 carries £30.37m of indicated new borrowing, £7.79m of maturing PWLB debt (£5m on 5 June 2026 and £2.79m on 31 March 2027) and potentially £19.25m of called LOBOs — close to £57m of borrowing decisions in one year, against a book that currently averages 4.63%. What rate does the MTFS assume, and what does each 1% above it cost?
entries.why: The council's own indicator puts a 1% rise at £432,000 of annual revenue. Three separate refinancings in one year is not three separate risks — it is one, taken three times.

threads.topic: The internal borrowing is running out of cash

entries.q: Balance sheet resources fall from £124.24m to £80.46m and then £63.19m over three years while the loans CFR rises from £169.69m to £193.26m. The liability benchmark more than doubles as a result. Is that fall in reserves a plan or a forecast?
entries.why: The liability benchmark moves on two assumptions — capital spend and reserves — and the reserves assumption is doing most of the work here. If reserves hold up, the borrowing need is smaller than £140m; if they fall faster, it is larger.

summary.text:
The annual Treasury Management Outturn Report for 2025-26, tabled at full Council on 22 July 2026 for noting. Identical content in the same words went to Cabinet the day before. A Welsh unitary whose treasury reporting is among the clearest we have read — and which has a decision sitting in it that the paper itself flags and does not resolve. At 31 March 2026 Bridgend held £99.72m of external borrowing against a £182.56m capital financing requirement, leaving £69.97m borrowed internally from its own balances. The whole book costs an average 4.63%.

£19.25m of it is LOBO debt — three loans taken in January 2004, carried at 4.65%, nominally running to 2054. The lender can reset the rate every January and July, and the council can refuse, which forces repayment. The outturn report, which went to full Council on 22 July, says plainly that the right 'may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026' and that the council 'will need to consider taking out new debt to replace them'. That date was 22 July — the day the paper was tabled. The council's own maturity table already treats the whole £19.25m as due within twelve months, which is why 27.32% of the book sits in the under-one-year bucket.

The arithmetic of replacing it is not subtle. The LOBOs cost 4.65%. The PWLB 10-year maturity rate is currently around 6%. On £19.25m that difference is roughly £264,000 a year, and the paper does not put a figure on it.

Investments are £44.50m, up from £36.75m, earning 4.73% at year end. £30.00m of that — 67% — is lent to other local authorities, at a weighted 5.29%, picked up over the year-end period when the council-to-council market pays best. Nothing is placed beyond 364 days. It is a deliberate and well-executed position; it is also two thirds of the portfolio in a sector whose credit story is the reason anyone reads these papers.

The direction of travel is the familiar one. The CFR rises from £182.56m to £203.77m in 2026-27, balance sheet resources fall from £124.24m to £80.46m and then £63.19m, and the liability benchmark — the least the council must borrow — goes from £55.45m to £121.90m to £140.07m across the same three years. Against that, £30.37m of new borrowing is indicated for 2026-27, before the £19.25m of LOBOs and the £7.79m of PWLB debt maturing in the same year are refinanced. MRP is already £6.508m.

Loan-book reconciliation ties to the pound: our file holds 24 PWLB loans totalling £78,327,849 at 4.7381% weighted, against the paper's £78.33m at 4.75% (matches on principal exactly and on rate to within a basis point). The balance-sheet identity CFR − external borrowing − OLTL = internal borrowing ties exactly to the council's own £69.97m figure.

officer.subject: Your Governance and Audit Committee on 24 September — the LOBO call date has passed
officer.body:
Dear Colleague,

Your Governance and Audit Committee meets on Thursday 24 September, and your own treasury outturn report names it as the committee responsible for scrutinising the strategy. We read council treasury papers and track PWLB rates every working day. We have been through Bridgend's outturn to 31 March 2026, which went to Council on 22 July.

It is one of the clearest treasury reports we have read this year — the liability benchmark table, the maturity structure and the counterparty detail are all there and they reconcile. This is not a list of things missing. It is the shortlist of questions we would expect a member who has read it properly to put to you.

Before any of that, one cross-check: we hold 24 PWLB loans for Bridgend totalling £78,327,849 at a weighted 4.7381%. Your Table 1 prints £78.33m at 4.75%. That ties to the pound on principal and to within a basis point on rate, which is the best a reader can do without your loan schedule.

The one with a date on it. Your report says the LOBO call right 'may be exercised at the next call date, July 2026' and that the council 'will need to consider taking out new debt to replace them'. The report went to Council on 22 July; the call date was 22 July, the same day. Whatever happened will have happened before this committee next sits, and the report as published leaves members without the answer.

The arithmetic is the part worth having ready. The £19.25m of LOBOs carries 4.65%. The PWLB 10-year maturity rate is currently around 6%. If the loans were called and replaced at around current levels, that is roughly £264,000 a year on £19.25m — against a whole-book average of 4.63% and total interest payable of £5.851m in 2025-26. A member who does that sum will want to know whether it lands in the MTFS.

Three we would expect beyond that:

1. On the refinancing load. 2026-27 carries £30.37m of indicated new borrowing on the liability benchmark, £7.79m of maturing PWLB debt (£5m on 5 June 2026 and £2.79m on 31 March 2027), and potentially the £19.25m of LOBOs — close to £57m of borrowing decisions in a single year. Your own indicator puts a 1% rise at £432,000 of annual revenue. Expect to be asked what rate the MTFS assumes and what each 1% above it costs.

2. On the counterparty concentration. £30.00m of the £44.50m investment book — 67% — sits with other local authorities at a weighted 5.29%. The year-end timing is well judged and the return shows it. The question is the size of the largest single exposure and what would trigger a reduction, because local authorities are the one counterparty class that carries no rating and the sector's credit story is the reason anyone reads these papers.

3. On the liability benchmark's reserves assumption. Balance sheet resources fall from £124.24m to £80.46m and then £63.19m across the forecast, which is what takes the benchmark from £55.45m to £121.90m to £140.07m. Members will reasonably ask whether that fall is a plan or a forecast, because it is doing more work in the borrowing number than the capital programme is.

Every figure above is from Bridgend's own report and we will send page references for any of them. Any indicative break-cost or replacement-rate number is exactly that — indicative. Only the DMO can quote.

A word on who we are, since this arrived unasked. PWLBtoday tracks PWLB rates every working day and reads the treasury papers of every council that publishes them. We do not sell treasury products and we do not advise on borrowing. There is a training library alongside it, for officers and for members. The courses your papers point to are listed with this email, each with the figure that put it there.

Sources: Treasury Management Outturn Report 2025-26, Bridgend County Borough Council, Council 22 July 2026 — cover report and Appendix A at democratic.bridgend.gov.uk documents s38285 and s38286.

With best wishes,

PWLBtoday
